enrichment.short_title: Coal subsidence depreciation and blight valuation
key_facts: Bolsover properties were damaged by a mining subsidence landslip and the Lands Tribunal awarded compensation under the Coal Mining Subsidence Act 1991.
The Coal Authority appealed the President's depreciation methodology for seven High Street properties and the Corderys cross-appealed the award for garden restoration at 43 New Station Road.
The President held the Authority's late section 10 election was invalid following McAreavey and assessed depreciation by distinguishing general area blight from damage-specific loss.
For the Corderys he capped garden restoration at £10,000 by reference to property value rather than reasonable reinstatement cost.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal to the Court of Appeal from Lands Tribunal awards on construction of the 1991 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Coal Authority appeal dismissed on depreciation; Corderys' cross-appeal allowed on remedial works quantum.
enrichment.ratio: Depreciation under sections 10 and 11 and Schedule 1 is measured by the effect of subsidence damage on the property's value, not general landslip blight; where no valid section 10 election has been made, remedial works must be assessed by reasonable practicability and satisfaction without capping cost by diminution in value.
legal_issues: How to measure depreciation under sections 10 and 11 when general blight affects the area
Whether fear of future damage may be reflected in depreciation valuations
Whether the Authority lost its right to elect a section 10 depreciation payment
Whether remedial works costs may be limited by reference to property value where no election was made

confidence.notes: Detailed statutory analysis, clear split outcomes on appeal and cross-appeal, and extensive valuation reasoning in the judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Uncross-examined defendant evidence at summary trial
key_facts: Carol Wilkinson was convicted of assault occasioning actual bodily harm by a district judge after a summary trial.
The prosecution played her police interview tape and she gave live evidence only to confirm that interview was true; she was not cross-examined.
Defence counsel argued the judge was bound to accept her unchallenged account, which if accepted would have acquitted her.
The district judge rejected her evidence and convicted; the case was stated for the Divisional Court.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Birmingham Magistrates' Court to the Administrative Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the district judge was entitled to reject the defendant's evidence despite the absence of cross-examination.
enrichment.ratio: A trial judge is not bound to accept unchallenged evidence; failure by prosecution counsel to cross-examine does not compel acceptance of the defence case, though prosecutors should make clear while a defendant is in the witness box that disputed evidence is not accepted.
legal_issues: Whether unchallenged defence evidence must be accepted at summary trial
The effect of prosecution failure to cross-examine the defendant
Whether the trial was fair where the defendant confirmed her interview account without further evidence
linked_authorities: R v Wood Green Crown Court ex parte Taylor

confidence.notes: Central legal questions and affirmative answers are clearly stated. Judge metadata in the source file lists Lord Hewitt and appears unreliable.

enrichment.short_title: Drink-driving blood sample evidence and continuity
key_facts: Simon Byrne was convicted of driving with excess alcohol after roadside and intoximeter tests at Basingstoke.
Discrepant breath readings led to a blood sample; prosecution relied on a section 9 statement from analyst Gavin Trotter, who was not a Home Secretary authorised analyst.
The district judge found continuity from matching bar-code references on police forms, the doctor's certificate and the analysed vial.
Defence challenges included custody sergeant comments discouraging independent analysis and use of a photocopied consent certificate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Basingstoke Magistrates' Court to the Administrative Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction upheld on all surviving grounds.
enrichment.ratio: Section 16 of the Road Traffic Offenders Act 1988 is permissive and does not exclude admissible expert evidence under section 9 of the Criminal Justice Act 1967; continuity of a blood sample may be inferred from consistent identifying codes across contemporaneous documents, and objections to admissibility must ordinarily be taken when evidence is tendered.
legal_issues: Whether analysis must be by an authorised analyst under section 16
Whether continuity of the blood sample was proved
Whether custody sergeant comments rendered the prosecution unfair
Whether a photocopy of the doctor's consent certificate was admissible

confidence.notes: Each case-stated question is answered explicitly with clear reasoning on admissibility and continuity.

enrichment.short_title: Drink-driving section 5(2) reverse burden read down
key_facts: Peter Sheldrake was convicted of being in charge of a motor vehicle with excess alcohol after providing a breath reading of 144 micrograms.
He failed to prove under section 5(2) that there was no likelihood of his driving while still over the limit.
The justices stated a case asking whether section 5(2) imposed a legal or evidential burden compatible with Article 6(2) after the Human Rights Act 1998.
Expert evidence indicated he would remain over the limit until about 11:40 am and cold weather increased the likelihood he might drive.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from North East Essex justices to a Divisional Court.
enrichment.outcome: Case stated answered: section 5(2) derogates from Article 6(2) and pursues a legitimate aim, but a legal burden is disproportionate and the provision must be read down under section 3(1) of the Human Rights Act 1998 to impose only an evidential burden.
enrichment.ratio: The 'it is a defence to prove' wording in section 5(2) of the Road Traffic Act 1988 ordinarily creates a legal burden that infringes the presumption of innocence; although road safety justifies some reverse burden, imposing the full persuasive burden is not proportionate and the section must be read compatibly as placing only an evidential burden on the accused.
legal_issues: Whether section 5(2) imposes a legal or evidential burden
Whether the reverse burden derogates from Article 6(2) of the Convention
Whether any derogation is justified and proportionate
Whether section 5(2) should be read down under section 3(1) of the Human Rights Act 1998

confidence.notes: The court's formal answers to the stated case and read-down holding are explicit. Judge metadata lists many names and appears inherited from citations rather than the panel.

enrichment.short_title: Theft by fake till refunds at retail outlet
key_facts: Richard Browbank, a retail assistant on the A34 near Winchester, was convicted of theft from his employer.
He keyed false refunds under a retail maps product code without removing corresponding cash, creating a surplus discovered on 26 October 2001.
Till records showed numerous similar refunds during his shifts using his PIN or training code 1111, without manager authorisation.
The justices found he removed the surplus when cashing up and that the money belonged to the employer.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from North East Hampshire justices to the Administrative Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; a reasonable tribunal properly directed could convict on the evidence.
enrichment.ratio: Where till records, PIN use, video evidence and refund patterns strongly indicate a dishonest system of false refunds, justices are entitled to infer appropriation even without stock checks proving that no goods were actually returned.
legal_issues: Whether the prosecution proved appropriation where refunds might theoretically correspond to returned goods
Whether there was no case to answer on theft

confidence.notes: Facts, issue and outcome are concise and clearly recorded, though the judgment contains limited authority citation.

enrichment.short_title: Oral section 152 notice to insurers' secretary
key_facts: After a 1998 road accident, the claimants obtained default judgment against the driver and sued his insurers.
No written section 152 notice was served; a trainee solicitor telephoned the insurers' solicitors saying proceedings were being issued and asking for the defendant's address.
The district judge found adequate notice had been given, but the circuit judge overturned that on recipient and sufficiency grounds.
The Court of Appeal restored the district judge's finding and ordered the insurers to be joined as second defendants.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal to the Court of Appeal from a circuit judge's decision on insurer liability under section 151/152.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; section 152 notice held sufficient; insurers joined as second defendants with liberty to apply to set aside deemed service.
enrichment.ratio: Notice under section 152(1)(a) of the Road Traffic Act 1988 need not be written or highly formal, but must sufficiently inform the insurer that proceedings are to be commenced; a legal secretary of the insurers' solicitors may be an appropriate recipient, and telling her that the claimant is 'now issuing' can satisfy the statutory requirement.
legal_issues: Whether notice of proceedings was given within seven days for section 152 purposes
Whether notice to a partner's legal secretary was notice to the insurer
Whether the telephone conversation was sufficient notice
What procedural orders should follow to protect insurer interests
index_terms: Herbert v Railway Passenger Assurance Co
linked_authorities: Herbert v Railway Passenger Assurance Co

confidence.notes: Issue, authorities summary and appeal outcome are clearly articulated by the Lord Chief Justice.

enrichment.short_title: Forestry Act felling without licence burden and mens rea
key_facts: Grundy and Co Excavations Ltd and Sean Parry were prosecuted for felling 86 trees at Sutton Weaver without a Forestry Commission licence.
They admitted felling the trees but said they acted on the landowner's permission and believed planning approval meant no Forestry Commission licence was needed.
The district judge ruled the prosecution bore only the act of felling and the defence bore a legal burden to prove an exception or licence applied.
The claimants sought judicial review to challenge those rulings on burden of proof and mens rea.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of magistrates' court rulings before trial, heard by a Divisional Court.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; reverse legal burden on exceptions and strict liability mens rea upheld as Convention-compatible.
enrichment.ratio: Sections 9 and 17 of the Forestry Act 1967 impose a legal reverse burden on the accused to prove on the balance of probabilities that felling fell within a section 9 exception or was authorised by licence; the offence is regulatory, strict liability is implied, and requiring a legal rather than evidential burden is necessary and proportionate under Article 6(2).
legal_issues: Who bears the burden of proving exceptions or a felling licence under section 17
Whether the reverse burden should be legal or evidential after the Human Rights Act 1998
Whether mens rea must be proved for an offence of felling without licence
Whether an honest and reasonable belief that no licence was required is a defence

confidence.notes: Detailed analysis of burden, mens rea and Convention compatibility with explicit conclusions. Judge metadata lists many historical names and appears unreliable.

enrichment.short_title: Port-of-entry student leave refused for maintenance
key_facts: A 43-year-old Zimbabwean citizen arrived at Gatwick without entry clearance and sought leave to enter as a student in health and social care.
He had last studied in 1979, paid first-year fees and part accommodation through a brother-in-law sponsor, and was refused leave on ability, intention to leave and maintenance grounds.
The immigration officer's report also doubted affordability given Zimbabwe's economic situation and the sponsor's responsibilities.
The judge held the officer was unreasonable on ability and intention to leave, but entitled to refuse on maintenance without further enquiry.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of a port immigration officer's refusal of leave to enter as a student.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; refusal upheld on the maintenance/funds ground despite partial success on other reasons.
enrichment.ratio: An applicant for leave to enter as a student at the port without prior entry clearance must satisfy all paragraph 57 requirements on the material before the officer; where maintenance funding from a sponsor is no more than assertion and plainly insufficient on the facts known, the officer may refuse without making further enquiries abroad.
legal_issues: Whether refusal on ability and intention to follow the course was Wednesbury unreasonable
Whether there was material to doubt intention to leave after studies
Whether the officer had to make further enquiries about the sponsor's finances before refusing on paragraph 57(vi)
Whether an unstated maintenance reason in the formal refusal letter invalidated the decision
linked_authorities: R v Chief Immigration Officer, Bradford Airport ex parte Hussain
R v Immigration Appeal Tribunal ex parte Shaikh
R v Secretary of State for the Home Department ex parte Bhambra

confidence.notes: Paragraph 57 analysis and split outcome on the three refusal reasons are clearly explained. Judge metadata lists Lord Parker CJ and appears unreliable.

enrichment.short_title: Compulsory purchase of vacant derelict house
key_facts: Newham made a compulsory purchase order for 72 Cranmer Road, a vacant derelict house owned by Terry Peart, to meet local housing need.
Peart proposed refurbishing the property himself for rental income to fund retirement, but the Inspector found he was unlikely to act within a reasonable time.
The Secretary of State confirmed the order after an inquiry; Peart challenged validity under section 23 of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981.
Maurice Kay J dismissed the challenge; Peart sought permission to appeal on Article 8 and Protocol 1 proportionality grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal from a section 23(2) Acquisition of Land Act 1981 challenge.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; application dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Confirmation of a compulsory purchase order under section 17 of the Housing Act 1985 is a proportionate interference with property rights where the property is vacant and derelict, local housing need is acute, and the owner's past inactivity supports the conclusion that private redevelopment would not occur within an acceptable timescale; Article 8 does not protect a right to invest in a particular property for retirement income.
legal_issues: Whether failure to consider Article 8 rendered the confirmation decision invalid
Whether past inactivity could be relied on when assessing future redevelopment
Whether the compulsory purchase disproportionately affected the owner's pension plans under Article 1 Protocol 1
Which permission test applies to section 23(2) Acquisition of Land Act appeals

confidence.notes: Grounds of challenge, first-instance reasoning and permission refusal are clearly set out. Judge metadata lists only Chadwick LJ though the panel included Auld LJ.

key_facts: Mr Erdogan, a Turkish Kurd aged 23, entered the UK clandestinely in December 2001 and claimed asylum with solicitor assistance.
He alleged mistreatment during military service and after arrest at a demonstration, plus police raids after he left Turkey.
The Special Adjudicator found his account largely consistent and plausible but rejected core allegations as fabricated and dismissed the appeal.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal refused permission to appeal; Erdogan sought judicial review of that refusal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of the Immigration Appeal Tribunal's refusal of permission to appeal from a Special Adjudicator asylum decision.
enrichment.ratio: There is no rule that a consistent and plausible asylum account must be accepted; an adjudicator may find an account incredible because identified core elements are fabricated, and that conclusion is not inconsistent with acknowledging general consistency or with the proper burden and standard of proof.
legal_issues: Whether an account described as consistent and plausible can lawfully be found incredible
Whether the adjudicator rejected the whole account or only core elements
Whether the IAT erred in refusing permission to appeal

confidence.notes: Credibility principles and dismissal are clearly explained, though the judgment cites little case law by name. Judge metadata lists Sir Richard Tucker though Lightman J gave the judgment.
